title: Sariputta on right view
hookLine: right view traced through nutriment, the truths and each link of the chain (MN 9)

cards: Good teachers have a move. They answer your question, then wait to see whether you'll ask a better one.
In MN 9, a group of monks keeps asking the same question, over and over, and their teacher, who for once isn't the Buddha, keeps finding a new answer.
Sixteen answers to one question, each going a little deeper, and the monks never seem to tire of asking.

teach.b: Sariputta was one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, known above all for wisdom; later commentaries call him the general of the teaching. In MN 9 he asks the monks: in what way is someone of right view?

And he answers: when they understand the unwholesome and its root, and the wholesome and its root. The roots of the unwholesome are greed, hatred and delusion; the roots of the wholesome are their absence.
But might there be another way? He answers again. Nutriment: the four kinds of food that keep beings going, their origin, their ending, and the way to their ending.
Another way? Dukkha, its origin, its ending, the way. Another?
Aging and death, the same four. Then birth. Then being, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six senses, name and form, consciousness, formations, ignorance, and at last the taints.
From the second round on, every round takes the same four steps: this thing, where it comes from, where it ends, and the way there.
It's the four noble truths used as a lens, and you can turn the lens on anything. That's right view in this discourse: less a belief to hold than a way of looking.
Trace anything back far enough and you find a link in a chain. And links, the discourse says, can be undone.

how: Theravada monastics study the Sammaditthi Sutta as a systematic account of right view, and Sariputta is honored across Buddhist traditions as the disciple foremost in wisdom.

o: right view: seeing a thing, its cause, its end, the way
seeing visions of the Buddha in meditation
holding the correct opinions about the Buddha

s: MN 9 is taught by the Buddha himself
Sariputta teaches it, to the monks.
Sariputta gives sixteen ways of being of right view
from the roots of the unwholesome to the taints.
right view in MN 9 is mainly a belief to hold
it's a way of looking: each thing, its origin, its ending, the way.

games.q: Sariputta gives a clear answer, and the monks say: good, friend. what do they do next?
o: go off to meditate on it
ask: might there be another way?
games.why: they ask for another way, sixteen times, and each time he finds one. the question keeps the teaching going deeper.

practice: Pick one feeling that's here right now, restlessness, a little sadness, an ache, and try Sariputta's four steps on it slowly: this is the feeling; where did it come from; when does it ease; what helps it ease? One link is enough.
Then let the steps go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Samma-ditthi, right view. The chief disciple shows right view as a way of looking: each thing, its origin, its ending, and the way.

orig.note: Pali sammā-diṭṭhi: right view, the name of MN 9.

carryVoice: Your line: Sariputta teaches. Any feeling can be traced back, one link at a time. Day four hundred nine, done.
